title: How to Identify the Correct Tense in Error Spotting Questions — Step-by-Step Method That Saves Marks
excerpt: Most aspirants lose easy marks in error spotting because they guess the tense instead of checking time markers and verb forms. This post gives you a clear 6-step classroom method so you can spot the right tense in under 30 seconds every time.
author: Balu Kandekar
content:
Nearly 40% of error-spotting mistakes in competitive exams come from tense confusion alone. One wrong verb form can cost you a full mark, and the examiner never explains why. This post shifts your thinking from “which tense sounds right?” to a fixed checking order that works every time.

Quick Answer: To identify the correct tense in error spotting, first locate the time marker (yesterday, since, already, while), then check whether the action is completed, ongoing, or habitual, and finally match the exact verb form. Ignore what “sounds natural” and follow the time-signal + form pair.

The Real Reason Tense Errors Keep Catching You

Here's what I've noticed after two decades of teaching this exact topic:

  • You read the sentence and pick the tense that “feels correct” instead of checking the time words.
  • You mix present perfect and simple past because both talk about past actions.
  • You forget that “since” and “for” force present perfect, while “ago” forces simple past.
  • You change a correct verb because the rest of the sentence looks complicated.
  • I know exactly how that feels — you walk out of the exam thinking “I should have got that one right.”

But here's what most people get wrong: they treat tense as a memory topic. It is not. It is a matching game between time signals and verb forms.

Three Mistakes That Cost Marks Every Year

1. Ignoring the time marker.
Students focus on the main verb and forget the small words that decide the tense. “Yesterday”, “last week”, “ago”, “since”, “already” are not decoration — they are instructions.

2. Confusing completed action with ongoing action.
Simple past shows a finished action. Present perfect shows a past action that still connects to now. Mixing them is the single biggest source of wrong answers.

3. Changing the correct form because of subject-verb agreement noise.
When the sentence is long, students start fixing number agreement and accidentally change a correct tense. The two errors are separate.

Common Mistakes Students Make

❌
Mistake 1: Ignoring the time marker

You look only at the verb and miss “yesterday” or “since”.

Wrong: She has gone to Mumbai yesterday.

Correct: She went to Mumbai yesterday.

❌
Mistake 2: Mixing simple past and present perfect

Both talk about past, but one needs a finished time and the other does not.

Wrong: I finished my work just now.

Correct: I have just finished my work.

❌
Mistake 3: Changing a correct tense while fixing agreement

Long sentences make you over-edit.

Wrong: The boys who lives next door has left.

Correct: The boys who live next door have left.

The Classroom Method That Works in 30 Seconds

Stop guessing. Follow this fixed order every time you see a tense error. The order itself prevents most mistakes.

Time SignalUsual TenseExample Form
yesterday / last week / agoSimple Pastwent, finished, saw
since / for / already / just / yetPresent Perfecthas gone, have finished
now / at present / currentlyPresent Continuousis working, are studying
while / when (two actions)Past Continuous + Simple Pastwas reading when the phone rang
every day / always / usuallySimple Presentgoes, works, studies

Step 1: Underline every time word. Circle “yesterday”, “since”, “already”, “while”, “ago”. These words decide the tense before you even look at the verb.

Step 2: Ask — is the action finished or still connected to now? Finished + past time marker = simple past. Connected to present = present perfect.

❌ She has left the office an hour ago.
✅ She left the office an hour ago. (ago forces simple past)

Step 3: Check if two actions happen at the same time. One long action + one short action usually needs past continuous + simple past.

Step 4: Look at the verb form itself. Has/have + V3 = present perfect. Was/were + V-ing = past continuous. Simple past is just V2.

Step 5: Confirm subject-verb agreement only after the tense is fixed. Never change a correct tense while fixing “is/are” or “has/have”.

Step 6: Read the full sentence once with your chosen form. If the time marker and the verb form match, you are done. Do not overthink.

Step-by-Step Strategy

1
Underline time markers first

Find yesterday, since, ago, already, while before touching the verb.

2
Decide finished vs connected to now

Finished + past time = simple past. Link to present = present perfect.

3
Check simultaneous actions

While/when often needs past continuous + simple past pair.

4
Match the exact verb form

V2 for simple past, has/have + V3 for present perfect, was/were + V-ing for continuous.

5
Fix agreement only after tense is set

Never change a correct tense while correcting is/are or has/have.

A Quick Turnaround Story

Ravi was stuck at 18–20 marks in English for months. His error-spotting score was always the weakest. He kept changing correct verbs because the sentences felt long. One evening I made him follow only the six steps above on twenty old questions. He stopped looking for “what sounds right” and started underlining time markers first. In the next mock he scored 26. The difference was not new grammar knowledge — it was a fixed checking order. You can do the same — here's how to start.

Expert Tips From the Classroom

  • Never start with the verb. Always start with the time word. The verb form is the last thing you decide.
  • Treat “ago” and “since” as opposite signals. “Ago” kills present perfect. “Since” demands it.
  • When two actions share the same time, one is usually continuous. The longer background action takes “was/were + V-ing”.
  • If you change more than one word, you are probably over-editing. Most tense errors need only one form change.

The Bottom Line

Tense errors in error spotting are not about memory. They are about matching a clear time signal to the correct verb form. Follow the six steps, ignore what “sounds natural”, and the marks start coming back.

Practice Questions (Exam Pattern Drills)

Q1 (SSC CGL Exam Pattern): She has been working in this office since five years.

**Summary:** Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: She has been working in this office for five years.

Explanation: “Since” needs a point of time (2019, Monday). “For” is used with a period of time (five years). This is covered in Step 1 and Step 2 — time marker decides the preposition and confirms present perfect continuous.

Q2 (Bank PO Exam Pattern): When I reached the station, the train already left.

**Summary:** Click to view step-by-step solution & rule

Answer: When I reached the station, the train had already left.

Explanation: Two past actions — the earlier one takes past perfect. “Already” also signals completion before another past moment. This matches Step 3 and Mistake 2 correction.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1. How do I quickly decide between simple past and present perfect?
Look for a finished time word. If you see “yesterday”, “last year”, “ago” — use simple past. If the action still connects to now or has no finished time — use present perfect.
Q2. Can “just” and “already” be used with simple past?
In exam English, “just” and “already” almost always take present perfect. Stick to that rule for error spotting.
Q3. What if there is no clear time marker in the sentence?
Check the meaning. Is the action finished and over, or does it still matter now? Also look at other verbs in the sentence for sequence clues.
Q4. Is past perfect still asked in recent exams?
Yes. Questions with two past actions (“when I reached… the train…”) still appear regularly. Learn the “earlier action = had + V3” rule.
Q5. Should I change the tense if the sentence only has a subject-verb agreement error?
No. Fix only the agreement. Changing a correct tense is a common over-editing mistake (see Mistake 3).
